title: Vital Signs & Exercise Monitoring
keywords: vitals vital signs bp blood pressure heart rate pulse respiratory rate spo2 oxygen saturation temperature rpe borg karvonen talk test exercise monitoring news2
summary: Measure pulse, blood pressure, breathing, SpO₂ and temperature properly — then use RPE, the talk test, pain monitoring and safety limits to dose and stop exercise safely.
ur: Pulse, BP, saans, SpO₂ aur temperature sahi tareeqe se lena — phir RPE, talk test aur safety limits se exercise ko safe rakhna.

sources.title: ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription (11th ed.)
Royal College of Physicians — National Early Warning Score (NEWS2)

goals.beginner: Know the normal adult values and why we measure them.
goals.intermediate: Measure every vital sign correctly and monitor exercise intensity.
goals.advanced: Spot measurement errors and abnormal responses to exercise.
goals.expert: Decide when to start, adjust or stop exercise — in clinic, ward and ICU.

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: 60–100 beats/min, regular

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Radial pulse with two fingers, counted for 30 s × 2 (a full 60 s if irregular); note rate, rhythm and volume

fields.label: Response to exercise
fields.value: Rises roughly in line with workload, then levels off at a steady state

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Using your thumb (you feel your own pulse) or counting 15 s with an irregular rhythm

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: Resting rate above about 120 or below 40 bpm, or heart rate falling as the workload rises
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Beta-blockers blunt the heart-rate response — prescribe intensity by RPE, not target heart rate.

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: Below 120/80 mmHg (hypertension from 140/90 in clinic)

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Seated 5 min, back supported, feet flat, arm supported at heart level, correct cuff; palpate systolic first, then auscultate Korotkoff I and V

fields.label: Response to exercise
fields.value: Systolic rises (about 10 mmHg per MET); diastolic stays the same or changes by less than 10 mmHg

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Cuff too small or arm below heart level (both over-read), talking, crossed legs, full bladder

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: Resting above 200/110 — don't start; during exercise systolic over 250 or diastolic over 115, or systolic falling more than 10 mmHg as work rises
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Measure both arms at the first visit — a difference over 15–20 mmHg suggests vascular disease; use the higher arm after that.

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: 12–20 breaths/min

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Count chest rises for 30 s × 2 without telling the patient — e.g. while still 'taking the pulse'

fields.label: Response to exercise
fields.value: Rises with intensity and settles within a few minutes of stopping

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Telling the patient you are counting — breathing changes when watched

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: Resting rate above about 30/min, or breathlessness out of proportion to the effort
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: A rising respiratory rate is one of the earliest signs of deterioration — it is part of every early-warning score (e.g. NEWS2).

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: 95–100% (target 88–92% in COPD with CO₂ retention)

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Probe on a warm finger, hand still and at heart level; wait for a steady reading with a good waveform

fields.label: Response to exercise
fields.value: Stays stable in healthy people; a fall of 4% or more is significant desaturation

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Nail polish, cold or poorly perfused fingers, movement, poor waveform

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: Below about 88–90% during exercise, unless the medical team set another target
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Oximeters can over-read in darker skin and in carbon monoxide poisoning — trust the patient and the trend, not one number.

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: About 36.1–37.2 °C (oral)

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Digital oral or tympanic thermometer, 15 minutes after any hot or cold drink

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Measuring straight after a hot or cold drink; poor probe placement

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: Fever of 38 °C or more — postpone exercise (infection raises the risk of myocarditis)
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Older adults may not mount a fever: new confusion or a rising pulse and breathing rate can be the first sign of infection.

atlas.title: Rating of perceived exertion (Borg 6–20)
atlas.subtitle: 12–13 ('somewhat hard') for moderate training; 14–16 for vigorous

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: 12–13 ('somewhat hard') for moderate training; 14–16 for vigorous

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Show the 6–20 scale and ask 'how hard is the whole body working?' near the end of each stage

fields.label: Response to exercise
fields.value: Climbs steadily with intensity; ×10 roughly matches heart rate in healthy young adults

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Asking about one tired muscle or breathing only; not explaining the scale before exercise

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: 17 or more ('very hard') in someone meant to train at moderate intensity — reduce the load
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: The best intensity guide with beta-blockers, pacemakers or atrial fibrillation, where heart rate misleads.

atlas.title: Breathlessness — modified Borg (CR10)
atlas.subtitle: Training usually aims for about 3–6 ('moderate' to 'severe') in pulmonary rehabilitation

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: Training usually aims for about 3–6 ('moderate' to 'severe') in pulmonary rehabilitation

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Ask the patient to rate breathlessness from 0 to 10 at rest, during and after exercise

fields.label: Response to exercise
fields.value: Rises with ventilation and returns to baseline within a few minutes

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Mixing it up with the 6–20 exertion scale

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: 7 or more, or breathlessness with chest pain, dizziness or desaturation
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Interval training keeps breathlessness lower than continuous training in severe COPD — the same work with less distress.

atlas.title: Talk test
atlas.subtitle: Moderate intensity = can talk in sentences but cannot sing

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: Moderate intensity = can talk in sentences but cannot sing

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Ask the patient to recite a standard passage (or count aloud) during exercise

fields.label: Response to exercise
fields.value: Speech gets harder as intensity passes the ventilatory threshold

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Asking yes/no questions only, so speech is never really tested

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: Cannot speak at all at a planned moderate intensity — the workload is too high
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Free, simple and closely matched to the ventilatory threshold — ideal for home programmes.

atlas.title: Pain (Numeric Rating Scale)
atlas.subtitle: 0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable; a change of about 2 points (30%) is clinically important

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: 0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable; a change of about 2 points (30%) is clinically important

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Ask for current, best and worst pain over the last 24 h on a 0–10 scale

fields.label: Response to exercise
fields.value: A rise to no more than about 5/10 that settles by the next morning is usually acceptable (pain-monitoring model)

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Leading the answer, or mixing pain intensity with distress

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: Pain above about 5/10 during exercise, or pain that has not settled by the next morning
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Silbernagel's pain-monitoring model guides tendon loading: adjust the next session by the 24-hour response.

atlas.title: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension check
atlas.subtitle: Systolic falls less than 20 mmHg and diastolic less than 10 mmHg on standing

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: Systolic falls less than 20 mmHg and diastolic less than 10 mmHg on standing

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Supine 5 min and measure; stand and measure again at 1 and 3 minutes; ask about dizziness

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Not resting supine first, or measuring only once after standing

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: A fall of 20+ systolic or 10+ diastolic within 3 minutes, or dizziness — sit down, hydrate, review medicines
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Common after bed rest and in Parkinson's, diabetes, spinal cord injury (T6 and above) and with antihypertensives — a key fall-risk factor.

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: Before exercise about 5.6–13.9 mmol/L (100–250 mg/dL)

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Fingerstick glucometer before exercise — and after it in people on insulin or sulfonylureas

fields.label: Response to exercise
fields.value: Usually falls during and for up to 24 hours after exercise in people on insulin

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Not checking before exercise in insulin users; forgetting delayed (night-time) hypoglycaemia

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: Below 5.6 mmol/L — eat 15–30 g carbohydrate first; above 13.9 with ketones — don't exercise; below 3.9 — stop and treat
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Treat hypoglycaemia with 15 g fast carbohydrate and re-check after 15 minutes (the 15–15 rule).

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Supine 10 min; Doppler systolic at both brachial arteries and at the ankle (dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial); ankle ÷ higher brachial

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Dividing by the lower brachial pressure; calcified arteries in diabetes falsely raise the result

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: Below 0.8 — avoid full compression; below 0.5 — severe disease, urgent vascular referral
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: Above 1.4 means incompressible (calcified) arteries — common in diabetes; use toe pressures instead.

fields.label: Normal value or target
fields.value: Colour returns in under 2 seconds

fields.label: How to measure
fields.value: Press the nail bed (or sternum) for 5 s with the limb at heart level, release and count

fields.label: Common errors
fields.value: Testing in a cold room or with the limb hanging down

fields.label: Stop / don't start
fields.value: Over 2–3 s with other signs of poor perfusion — escalate
fields.ask: When does {title} mean stop (or don't start) exercise?

fields.label: Clinical note
fields.value: A cold, pale, pulseless, painful limb with slow refill is acute limb ischaemia — an emergency.

concepts.title: Why physios measure vitals
concepts.body: Vitals give a **baseline**, keep exercise **safe**, and show how the body **responds** to load. Measure **before** you start, **during** the session and **after** recovery.
concepts.ur: Exercise se pehle, dauran aur baad vitals lena — taake baseline, safety aur response teeno pata chalein.

concepts.title: Normal adult values at rest
concepts.body: Learn these by heart — every station starts here.

concepts.title: Blood pressure, step by step
concepts.body: Most BP errors are set-up errors.
bullets: Rest seated 5 minutes, back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed
Cuff bladder covers about 80% of the arm circumference; arm at heart level
Palpate the radial pulse while inflating — note where it disappears (estimated systolic)
Inflate 20–30 mmHg above that, deflate 2–3 mmHg per second
Korotkoff I (first sound) = systolic; V (sounds disappear) = diastolic

concepts.title: Three ways to set intensity
concepts.body: Use heart-rate reserve (Karvonen), RPE or the talk test — together when you can.

concepts.title: Abnormal responses to exercise
concepts.body: Know what 'wrong' looks like before it happens.

head: Response
What you see
Action
rows: Systolic falls > 10 mmHg as work rises
Heart rate fails to rise with work

concepts.title: Medicines that change the numbers
concepts.body: Check the drug chart before you interpret anything.
bullets: Beta-blockers — lower resting and peak heart rate: use RPE
Antihypertensives/diuretics — post-exercise and postural hypotension: cool down gradually
Insulin/sulfonylureas — hypoglycaemia during and after exercise: check glucose
Bronchodilators — take before exercise in asthma/COPD

concepts.title: Stop exercise immediately if…
concepts.body: Symptoms beat numbers. Stop and assess if any appear:
bullets: Chest pain or pressure (angina), new palpitations
Dizziness, confusion, unsteadiness, pallor or cyanosis
Severe breathlessness or wheeze out of proportion to effort
Systolic BP falling with increasing work, or SpO₂ below about 88–90%

concepts.title: Ward and ICU: early mobilisation
concepts.body: Many units use traffic-light criteria before mobilising. Typical safe ranges include **heart rate 40–130 bpm, mean arterial pressure 60–110 mmHg, SpO₂ ≥ 88–90%, respiratory rate below about 30–35** — always follow your local protocol and the medical team. Use **NEWS2** to recognise deterioration on the ward.

questions.prompt: Normal adult resting heart rate is…
questions.explain: 60–100 bpm at rest.

questions.prompt: Normal adult respiratory rate is…
options: 25–35 breaths/min
40–60 breaths/min
4–8 breaths/min
12–20 breaths/min
questions.explain: 12–20 per minute.

questions.prompt: When should vitals be measured around exercise?
options: Before, during and after
Only after
Only if the patient complains
Only before
questions.explain: Baseline, response and recovery.

questions.prompt: Where do you usually feel the pulse in clinic?
options: Femoral artery
Ulnar artery at the elbow
Radial artery at the wrist
Popliteal artery
questions.explain: Radial pulse — lateral wrist, two fingers.

questions.prompt: Karvonen: age 40, resting HR 70, intensity 60%. Target HR?
options: 112 bpm
136 bpm
108 bpm
180 bpm

questions.prompt: Diastolic blood pressure is recorded at…
options: Korotkoff phase V (sounds disappear)
The loudest sound
When the cuff is fully inflated
Korotkoff phase I
questions.explain: Phase V = disappearance of sounds.

questions.prompt: Moderate intensity on the Borg 6–20 scale is about…
questions.explain: 12–13 = 'somewhat hard'.

questions.prompt: Why count breaths without telling the patient?
options: People change their breathing when they know it is being counted
It is quicker
It is a legal requirement
So you can count for only 5 s
questions.explain: Awareness alters breathing pattern.

questions.prompt: A cuff that is too small for the arm will…
options: Under-read blood pressure
Over-read blood pressure
Only affect heart rate
Make no difference
questions.explain: Small cuff = falsely high.

questions.prompt: During a graded exercise session the systolic BP falls from 150 to 132 mmHg as the workload increases. This is…
options: Exertional hypotension — stop
Measurement error — ignore
A hypertensive response
Normal
questions.explain: Systolic should rise with work; a fall > 10 mmHg is a stop sign.

questions.prompt: A patient on bisoprolol (a beta-blocker) — the best way to guide intensity is…
options: Target heart rate from 220 − age
Respiratory rate only
SpO₂
RPE (and the talk test)
questions.explain: Beta-blockers blunt heart rate.

questions.prompt: Diastolic BP during exercise normally…
options: Stays the same or changes by less than 10 mmHg
Doubles
Falls to zero
Rises 10 mmHg per MET
questions.explain: It's systolic that rises with workload.

questions.case: Pre-exercise check: BP 214/112 mmHg, no symptoms, forgot his tablets.
questions.prompt: What do you do?
options: Start gently and monitor
Proceed — he has no symptoms
Don't start exercise; re-check after rest and arrange medical review
Exercise to bring the BP down
questions.explain: Resting BP over 200/110 is a contraindication to exercise.

questions.case: COPD patient walking: SpO₂ drops from 93% to 85%, breathlessness 7/10.
questions.prompt: Best action?
options: Ignore — COPD patients always desaturate
Increase the speed to finish sooner
Stop and rest; resume with intervals and oxygen as prescribed
Keep going to build tolerance
questions.explain: Below 88% with severe breathlessness = stop and recover.

questions.case: Type 1 diabetes, insulin this morning; pre-exercise glucose 4.8 mmol/L (86 mg/dL).
questions.prompt: What do you do?
options: Start exercise immediately
Give insulin
Cancel physiotherapy for the week
Give 15–30 g carbohydrate, re-check, then start
questions.explain: Below 5.6 mmol/L: carbohydrate first to prevent hypoglycaemia.

questions.case: First day out of bed after surgery: BP lying 128/76; standing 1 min 102/64, patient dizzy.
questions.prompt: Interpretation and action?
options: Hypertensive crisis
Normal response — keep walking
Orthostatic hypotension — sit/lie down, then progress gradually (sitting → standing) with hydration and leg exercises
Hypoglycaemia
questions.explain: A 26 mmHg systolic fall with symptoms = orthostatic hypotension.

questions.case: Cardiac rehab: chest tightness at RPE 13 that eases with rest; HR and BP normal.
questions.prompt: Best action?
options: Teach diaphragmatic breathing and carry on
Stop, monitor and report — angina symptoms override normal numbers
Continue — the numbers are normal
Increase the intensity
questions.explain: Symptoms beat numbers: new chest tightness is a stop sign.

questions.case: Pulse oximeter reads 99% in a confused patient rescued from a house fire.
questions.prompt: Why be cautious?
options: Carbon monoxide makes oximeters over-read — the patient may be hypoxic
The probe must be on the toe
Confusion raises SpO₂
99% is always accurate
questions.explain: Carboxyhaemoglobin is read as oxygenated haemoglobin.

questions.prompt: Compression therapy?
options: Full compression is safe
Compression is mandatory
ABPI doesn't matter
Avoid full compression — refer for vascular assessment
questions.explain: ABPI < 0.8 = arterial disease; full compression could cause ischaemia.

questions.case: Achilles tendinopathy loading: pain 3/10 during hops, 4/10 next morning (baseline 2/10).
questions.prompt: Next session?
options: Double the load
Stop all loading
Continue the same load — the response is acceptable
Switch to complete rest for 6 weeks
questions.explain: Pain ≤ 5/10 that settles within 24 h is acceptable in the pain-monitoring model.

questions.case: Day 2 after a large stroke, ward patient: HR 138 bpm at rest, RR 28/min, temperature 38.4 °C.
questions.prompt: Mobilisation today?
options: Mobilise as planned
Hold active mobilisation, escalate to the medical team (possible sepsis/aspiration)
Start a treadmill session
Sit out of bed for 2 hours
questions.explain: Tachycardia, tachypnoea and fever = deterioration; escalate first.

questions.prompt: Which finding is a reason to stop exercise even when HR and BP look normal?
options: Mild sweating
RPE 12
Heart rate rising with workload
New dizziness, confusion or pallor
questions.explain: Signs of poor perfusion override the numbers.

cards.back: Systolic falls less than 20 mmHg and diastolic less than 10 mmHg on standing

cards.front: Correct way to measure Orthostatic (postural) hypotension check?
cards.back: Supine 5 min and measure; stand and measure again at 1 and 3 minutes; ask about dizziness

cards.front: Common error when measuring Orthostatic (postural) hypotension check?
cards.back: Not resting supine first, or measuring only once after standing

cards.front: When does Orthostatic (postural) hypotension check mean stop (or don't start) exercise?
cards.back: A fall of 20+ systolic or 10+ diastolic within 3 minutes, or dizziness — sit down, hydrate, review medicines

cards.front: Normal value or target for Blood glucose (diabetes)?
cards.back: Before exercise about 5.6–13.9 mmol/L (100–250 mg/dL)

cards.front: Correct way to measure Blood glucose (diabetes)?
cards.back: Fingerstick glucometer before exercise — and after it in people on insulin or sulfonylureas

cards.front: Expected response of Blood glucose (diabetes) to exercise?
cards.back: Usually falls during and for up to 24 hours after exercise in people on insulin

cards.front: Common error when measuring Blood glucose (diabetes)?
cards.back: Not checking before exercise in insulin users; forgetting delayed (night-time) hypoglycaemia

cards.front: When does Blood glucose (diabetes) mean stop (or don't start) exercise?
cards.back: Below 5.6 mmol/L — eat 15–30 g carbohydrate first; above 13.9 with ketones — don't exercise; below 3.9 — stop and treat

cards.front: Normal value or target for Ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI)?
Correct way to measure Ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI)?
cards.back: Supine 10 min; Doppler systolic at both brachial arteries and at the ankle (dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial); ankle ÷ higher brachial

cards.front: Common error when measuring Ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI)?
cards.back: Dividing by the lower brachial pressure; calcified arteries in diabetes falsely raise the result

cards.front: When does Ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI) mean stop (or don't start) exercise?
cards.back: Below 0.8 — avoid full compression; below 0.5 — severe disease, urgent vascular referral

cards.front: Normal value or target for Capillary refill time?
cards.back: Colour returns in under 2 seconds

cards.front: Correct way to measure Capillary refill time?
cards.back: Press the nail bed (or sternum) for 5 s with the limb at heart level, release and count

cards.front: Common error when measuring Capillary refill time?
cards.back: Testing in a cold room or with the limb hanging down

cards.front: When does Capillary refill time mean stop (or don't start) exercise?
cards.back: Over 2–3 s with other signs of poor perfusion — escalate
